## Model Comparison and Recommendation

Both models are evaluated on identical held-out test sets across four configurations, shown in @tbl-model-comparison. As described in the SVM section, the SVR had to be fitted on subsamples of 20,000 and 50,000 rows, while the network could be trained on the full data of 1.1 million rows for community areas at 1h and 6.8 million for census tracts. Part of the gap between the two models therefore reflects how much data each could use. We treat this as a property of the methods. Being able to use a dataset of this size is one of the advantages of the neural network.

| Configuration | SVR R² | NN R² | SVR nMAE | NN nMAE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Community area, 1h | 0.84 | 0.90 | 0.45 | 0.34 |
| Census tract, 1h | 0.63 | 0.87 | 1.95 | 0.42 |
| Community area, 4h | 0.91 | 0.93 | 0.29 | 0.25 |
| Community area, 1d | 0.93 | 0.93 | 0.23 | 0.24 |

: Comparison of SVR and NN across matched spatio-temporal configurations {#tbl-model-comparison}

The SVR row for each configuration is its selected variant: community areas at 4h use the log1p target with an RBF kernel, the other three use the untransformed target with a polynomial kernel, all with target encoding. nMAE is reported on a single definition for both models: the mean absolute error divided by mean test demand, so the two columns are on the same scale.^[Both models are scored on the identical held-out test sets (235,897 rows for community areas at 1h, 1,449,082 for census tracts at 1h, 58,985 at 4h and 9,840 at 1d), so the normalizing denominator is the same for each pair.]

On R² the two models converge as the time window widens. At 1d both reach 0.93 and at 4h the gap is 0.91 for the SVR against 0.93 for the NN. The difference in performance shows at finer resolutions. For the smallest temporal buckets of 1h, the SVR reaches 0.84 for community areas against the 0.90 of the NN. In the spatial dimension, the SVR falls to 0.63 for census tracts (at 1h) while the network holds 0.87. The SVR only keeps up with the network when the buckets are aggregated into larger ones, while the network stays stable across resolutions. The normalized MAE tells a similar story. The network has the lower error at every resolution except the daily one, where the two are effectively tied (0.24 against 0.23), and the SVR is marginally ahead. The largest gap by far is on census tracts, where the SVR error exceeds mean demand (1.95) while the network stays at 0.42.

Neither model is simpler to build. The SVR needed target encoding, log1p, and a custom scorer. The network replaces the first with embeddings and avoids the other two by training on an L1 loss, which is robust to the skewed target, but it requires architecture search, dropout, and learning-rate tuning instead. What separates them is scale. The SVR cannot use the full dataset, and that shows at the fine resolutions where the extra data matters most.

A more direct test is whether either model beats an operator working without one. We assume a fleet operator would rely on historical averages per community area, 4h bucket, and weekday/weekend split, essentially saying "on a Tuesday between 8 and 12 in community area 10 we expect 8.2 trips". This rule of thumb reaches an nMAE of 0.31 on the test set. The SVR improves on it only marginally (0.29, a reduction of 5.7 percent), most likely because it only sees a fraction of the training data, while the network reaches 0.25, an improvement of roughly 18 percent. For the SVR the modelling effort barely pays off against a simple historical average, while for the network the gain is substantial. The network is therefore the model we would put into production.
In practical terms, the network predicts demand within five trips of the actual count in roughly 83% of all 4h test windows (see @tbl-nn-accuracy).

That leaves the question of which resolution to run it at. We recommend community areas in four-hour windows (R² 0.93, nMAE 0.25). Daily forecasts score marginally better on nMAE and marginally worse on R² (0.93, nMAE 0.24) but are too coarse for a fleet operator to work with, while hourly forecasts add noise without adding planning value. Census tracts were considered for their finer spatial detail but rejected. Fewer than half of the records contain census tract information (see Chapter 1), and many tracts generate fewer than one trip per window, which is too granular to allocate vehicles against. Community areas are small enough to act on. The average community area in Chicago covers roughly three square miles,^[Chicago comprises 77 community areas across roughly 227 square miles (U.S. Census Bureau).] which a taxi can cross in under fifteen minutes.
